prenatal exposure to undernutrition during early fetal life was found to be associated with an older‐appearring brain in late adulthood.

prenatal exposure to maternal nutrient restriction was linked to a status of premature neurodegeneration during late adulthood in males, in the absence of growth restriction at birth or vascular pathology in late life, and that this effect could be tracked by an innovative biomarker of brain aging.

exposure to maternal nutrient restriction in early gestation is associated with a status resembling premature brain aging during adulthood, as well being explained by birth‐ and health characteristics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of prenatal exposure to undernutrition during early‐gestation on brain aging during late‐adulthood.
the question of how early‐life environmental factors influence the development of the brain and its function.
the effects of early‐life exposure to maternal undernutrition on individual brain aging during late‐life.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the status of premature aging in participants exposed during early gestation to the Dutch famine occurred in the absence both of fetal growth restriction as well as vascular damage in late‐life, indicating a direct effect of prenatal undernutrition on brain structure, which might be mediated by epigenetic mechanisms.

our findings on exposure to prenatal malnutrition during early gestational age being associated with a premature brain aging status during late adulthood are strongly supporting the crucial importance of sufficient nutrient supplies during pregnancy.

the Dutch famine cohort study has provided evidence of premature brain aging, as well as a biomarker for brain aging that is able to detect the impact of prenatal exposure to maternal nutrient restriction on individual brain aging during late‐life.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
prenatal malnutrition is linked with older‐appearing male brains in late‐life, and that the variance in brain aging in males is explained to a large extent by birth and late‐life characteristics.

the Dutch famine cohort is a unique opportunity to understand the effects of early‐life adversity and how this may impact brain aging and health in late‐life, which may be applicable in other populations.
prenatal undernutrition is linked to premature brain aging in the male sample by 4.4 years, which occurred in the absence or vascular pathology and fetal growth restriction at the time of birth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
prenatal exposure to undernutrition during early‐gestation is associated with premature brain aging during later‐life.
prenatal undernutrition during pregnancy is linked to premature brain aging in adulthood, as well.
